That site includes references to Joelle Barral and Nikola Stikov’s work in fitting these kinds of data.

Barral:  A robust methodology for in vivo T1 mapping

Stikov:  On the accuracy of T1 mapping: Searching for common ground

## MR pulse sequence diagrams:  the measured signals depend on multiple factors

![MR pulse sequence diagrams:  the measured signals depend on multiple factors.](images/ch10/mr-pulse-sequence-diagrams-the-measured-signals-de.png){#fig-ch10-mr-pulse-sequence-diagrams-the-measured-signals-de}

The device programming is based on creating different pulse sequences.
Two examples of pulse sequences are shown here.
The pulse sequences themselves can be quite different to emphasize different features of the brain.
Equally important, the parameters of the pulse sequences can be adjusted to highlight certain differences and diminish others.

## Blood oxygenation influences transverse magnetization relaxation rate(Huettel et al., Fig 7.1; After Thulborn, 1982)

![Blood oxygenation influences transverse magnetization relaxation rate(Huettel et al., Fig 7.1; After Thulborn, 1982).](images/ch10/blood-oxygenation-influences-transverse-magnetizat.png){#fig-ch10-blood-oxygenation-influences-transverse-magnetizat}

Figure 7.1 Effects of blood deoxygenation upon MR relaxation constants. Shown are the differential effects of blood deoxygenation upon transverse and longitudinal relaxation times, as expressed by the constants 1/T2 (blue circles) and 1/T1 (red circles). The xaxis indicates the square of the proportion of deoxygenated blood. Note that oxygenation increases from left to right. Clearly evident is the fact that 1/T2 decreases with increasing oxygenation; that is, the more deoxygenated hemoglobin that is present, the shorter the T2. Note that T1 is not affected by blood oxygenation level. (After Thulborn et al., 1982.)

## BOLD T2* curves: Quantitative

![BOLD T2* curves: Quantitative.](images/ch10/bold-t2-curves-quantitative.png){#fig-ch10-bold-t2-curves-quantitative}

% some constants
te = 29;       % te for spiral-out
readout = 33;  % duration of readout

% time in milliseconds
x = 0:200;

% te_rest is the rest-state T2*; te_active is the active-state T2*; (at 3 T)
te_rest = [44.9 46.1 43.9 46.1];
te_active = [46.4 48.7 45.4 46.1+.93];

% let's just take the mean
te_rest = mean(te_rest);
te_active = mean(te_active);

% look at signal decay
figure; hold on;
plot(x,exp(-x./te_rest),'r-');
plot(x,exp(-x./te_active),'g-');
straightline([te te+readout],'v','b-');
xlabel('time (ms)');
ylabel('signal');
legend({'rest' 'active'});
title('signal decay');

% look at difference between active and rest
figure; hold on;
plot(x,exp(-x./te_active)-exp(-x./te_rest),'r-');
straightline([te te+readout],'v','b-');
xlabel('time (ms)');
ylabel('signal difference');
title('difference in signal between active and rest');

% look at the percent change relative to rest
figure; hold on;
plot(x,(exp(-x./te_active)./exp(-x./te_rest) - 1) * 100,'r-');
straightline([te te+readout],'v','b-');
xlabel('time (ms)');
ylabel('percent change');
title('percent change relative to rest');

## Real BOLD T2* curves difference:  Quantitative

![Real BOLD T2* curves difference:  Quantitative.](images/ch10/real-bold-t2-curves-difference-quantitative.png){#fig-ch10-real-bold-t2-curves-difference-quantitative}
